chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Dawud al-Sarri, who said:

Al-Tayyib (peace be upon him) said: 'O Dawud, indeed all people are our mawali (clients/freemen), so it is permissible for us to buy and free them.' I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, a certain man said to his slave whom he had freed, 'Sell yourself to me so that I may buy you.' He said: 'It is permissible, but he only acquires his wilayah (guardianship/clientage).'

key_terms.بِعْنِي نَفْسَكَ: Sell yourself to me (a contract of self-sale)
key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a common phrase of respect in hadith)
key_terms.مَوَالٍ: Mawali (clients or freemen under the patronage of a master or Imam)
key_terms.وِلَاءَهُ: His wilayah (guardianship, clientage, or right of patronage)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling on a freed slave selling himself back to his former master in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Tayyib (peace be upon him) elucidates the unique juridical status of the Imams as universal *mawali* (patrons), granting them the authority to purchase and emancipate individuals directly. The dialogue with Dawud al-Sarri specifically addresses the validity of a freed slave selling himself back to his former master, clarifying that such a transaction transfers *wilayah* (clientage/guardianship) rather than reinstating full slavery, a nuance critical to Shia fiqh of manumission.
